claims.text: At the September meeting the Committee delivered a hawkish action, hiking the policy rate by a quarter point, which sets the baseline for the next decision.
claims.quote: The Committee decided to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point to 3-3/4 to 4 percent, in support of the Federal Reserve's dual mandate.

claims.text: The September statement frames inflation as still elevated and the action as serving a faster return to target, signaling continued tightening bias.
claims.quote: Inflation remains elevated. Today's policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability.

claims.text: The September decision was unanimous, a hawkish hardening from July when three members had dissented in favor of a hike.
claims.quote: The Federal Open Market Committee approved the following statement for release by a 12 – 0 vote:

claims.text: The SEP median points to a rate above the current midpoint by year-end, consistent with at least one further hike before holding, implying a hawkish-but-limited path.
claims.quote: The median participant judges that the appropriate federal funds rate to be 4.1 percent at the end of this year and to remain there next year.

claims.text: The Chairman characterized risks as skewed toward inflation, supporting a hawkish lean.
claims.quote: Inflation risks are to the upside while labor risks are roughly balanced.

claims.text: The Chairman declined to pre-commit to further moves, tempering the hawkish signal with uncertainty about the next step.
claims.quote:
I’m
not going to prejudge any future decisions we make.

claims.text: The July minutes show many participants viewed further tightening as likely if inflation did not fall, a hawkish conditional stance carried into subsequent meetings.
claims.quote: Many participants assessed that policy tightening would likely be necessary if inflation did not decline.

claims.text: Vice Chair Jefferson saw inflation risks tilted up heading into October, a hawkish read from a core voter.
claims.quote: I view risks to my inflation forecast as tilted to the upside due to recent geopolitical developments and stronger-than-anticipated aggregate demand.

claims.text: Jefferson conditioned any future move on incoming data rather than pre-committing, a neutral/data-dependent note.
claims.quote: any future adjustments in policy should be determined by carefully examining trends in the data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks

claims.text: Governor Barr said he did not yet see a clear disinflation trend, supporting a hawkish inclination.
claims.quote: I don't yet see a clear trend toward a timely return to 2 percent.

claims.text: Governor Cook framed her commitment around returning inflation to target while protecting the labor market, consistent with a mildly hawkish stance.
claims.quote: I am committed to returning inflation to our objective while preserving the strength in the labor market.

output.summary: The committee's own communications lean hawkish into the October 28 decision. In September the Committee unanimously (12-0) raised the target range by a quarter point to 3-3/4 to 4 percent, hardening from July's 9-3 vote where dissenters had wanted a hike. The September statement still calls inflation \"elevated\" and frames the action as supporting a \"timelier return\" to 2 percent, while the SEP median of 4.1 percent at year-end sits above the current midpoint, implying room for at least one more hike before holding. The press conference cites upside inflation risks, and speeches from Jefferson (inflation risks \"tilted to the upside\"), Barr (no \"clear trend toward a timely return to 2 percent\"), and Cook reinforce a tightening bias. Offsetting this somewhat, the Chairman explicitly refused to \"prejudge any future decisions,\" the SEP median shows the rate holding next year, and Jefferson emphasized data-dependent future adjustments—so the hawkish tilt is moderate rather than strong. Net tilt: +5 bp.
